questions.q: What is the original medium of delivery for G.B. Shaw's essay "Freedom" and how do you know from the text?
questions.a: The essay was originally a radio broadcast ("wireless talk"). The text explicitly states: "I am never controversial over the wireless" and "this is why we listen to wireless talks about it." A wrong answer (e.g., "it was a newspaper article") reveals the student missed the medium-specific clues and cannot distinguish between written and spoken non-fiction forms.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the historical setting of 1930s Britain influences Shaw's examples and arguments in "Freedom."
questions.a: Shaw references British historical events (Magna Carta, Spanish Armada, Charles I, Bill of Rights, Waterloo, Trafalgar) to expose how the ruling class uses a distorted version of history to legitimize their power. He also mentions contemporary issues: "rack-rented, underpaid" workers, the dole, trade unions, and the Russian Revolution (1922). A wrong answer that only lists events without linking them to Shaw's critique of class propaganda shows the student cannot connect setting to rhetorical purpose.

questions.q: Identify three specific linguistic features in Krishnamurti's talk that create an atmosphere of intimate urgency, and explain the effect of each.
questions.a: 1. Direct second-person address ("you are all young", "your parents", "your examinations") — creates personal confrontation. 2. Rhetorical questions ("Do you have any feeling for them?", "Are you actually so blinded?") — forces self-examination. 3. Present-tense immediacy ("you are enclosed", "there is a conflict going on") — makes the struggle feel current and inescapable. A wrong answer that only lists "questions" without explaining their persuasive function shows superficial understanding of atmosphere creation.

questions.q: Compare the atmospheres of Shaw's and Krishnamurti's essays. How does each author's tone serve their distinct purpose?
questions.a: Shaw uses satirical irony, hyperbole, and provocative generalizations ("the amazing thing is that you are fool enough to believe them") to shock a complacent mass audience into recognizing their exploitation. Krishnamurti uses quiet intensity, repetitive questioning, and philosophical reasoning to awaken individual students' critical intelligence. Shaw's atmosphere is public, combative, and political; Krishnamurti's is private, meditative, and psychological. A wrong answer that says "both are serious" misses the strategic difference between public provocation and private inquiry.

questions.q: Evaluate: Which essay's setting makes its argument more accessible to a modern Indian Class 12 student? Justify with two specific textual reasons.
questions.a: Krishnamurti's talk is more accessible because: (1) its school setting and direct address to youth ("you are all young") mirrors the student's own context, and (2) its focus on internal psychological struggle (fear, conformity, tradition) transcends the specific 1930s British political references that dominate Shaw's essay. A wrong answer that picks Shaw because "he uses simpler words" ignores the cultural-historical distance of his allusions (Magna Carta, Eton, British wage-slaves) and misjudges accessibility.

questions.q: Write a 50-word "atmosphere annotation" for the opening paragraph of Shaw's essay, describing the tone and its intended effect on the 1930s radio listener.
questions.a: The opening adopts a deceptively reasonable, almost conversational tone ("Evidently a person who can do what he likes...") that lures the listener into agreement before dismantling the very concept of perfect freedom. This disarming rationality establishes Shaw as a fellow thinker, not a preacher, making the subsequent radical critique of "wage slavery" more palatable to a conservative radio audience. A poor annotation merely labels the tone "informative" without analyzing its strategic manipulation.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Setting in non-fiction refers to the historical, cultural, and immediate context of the text's production and reception — including the time period, ______ location, intended audience, and medium of delivery.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're scrolling through a podcast app: a political commentary episode from the 1930s sounds ______ different from a modern TED Talk for students.
What is Setting in non-fiction? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Setting in non-fiction refers to the historical, cultural, and immediate context of the text's production and reception — including the time period, geographical location, intended audience, and medium of delivery.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine you're scrolling through a podcast app: a political commentary episode from the ______s sounds completely different from a modern TED Talk for students.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Setting in non-fiction?
questions.a: Students often believe non-fiction texts have no "setting" because they lack fictional world-building, or that "atmosphere" only applies to stories with sensory descriptions.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify the specific historical context and original medium of each essay, explain how the setting shapes the author's arguments and rhetorical choices, and analyze the distinctive atmosphere (tone, mood, emotional register) created by linguistic features in both Shaw's and Krishnamurti's pieces, supporting each point.
